analysis.one_liner: Extends ACA premium subsidies at shrinking levels, routes them into savings accounts, and forces hospitals to post prices.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill introduced in December 2025 would extend enhanced ACA premium credits through 2031 while phasing them down, steer the money into health savings accounts, restrict coverage of abortion and gender-transition care, and tighten hospital price transparency rules — it has one sponsor, no cosponsors, and sits in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would keep enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits alive through 2031, but shrink them 20% a year starting in 2028 and require every enrollee to pay at least $10–$40 a month out of pocket. It would also raise the income cap for credits to 700% of the poverty line, move the subsidy payments into special health savings accounts, bar those accounts and marketplace plans from covering gender-transition procedures or abortion, put federal money behind cost-sharing reductions and state reinsurance programs, and toughen price transparency requirements for hospitals, labs, imaging providers, and surgery centers.
analysis.who_benefits: Marketplace enrollees who would otherwise lose or see sharply higher premiums when the enhanced credits phase down — the bill delays and softens that phaseout and extends eligibility to households earning up to 700% of the poverty line. States that want federal grants for reinsurance programs also gain a funding stream. Insurers gain restored cost-sharing-reduction payments and market-stabilization money.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the enhanced premium tax credits (set to expire after 2025) through 2031, with a phasedown that reduces the enhanced portion by 20% per year starting after 2027.
Raises the income ceiling for premium credits from 400% to 700% of the federal poverty line for 2027 through 2031.
Directly appropriates money for cost-sharing reduction payments, which the bill directs to issuers to reduce premiums for people eligible for those reductions.

Appropriates $500 million for fiscal 2027 and $5 billion each for fiscal 2028–2030 for state reinsurance and 'invisible high-risk pool' programs, with a federal backstop for states that do not set one up.

Requires hospitals, clinical labs, imaging providers, and ambulatory surgical centers to post standard charges, negotiated rates, and discounted cash prices — and to accept the discounted cash price as payment in full — with per-day civil penalties for noncompliance.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the extended credits, the cost-sharing reductions, and the $15.5 billion in reinsurance and stabilization grants. Hospitals, labs, and imaging providers bear compliance costs and exposure to daily penalties. Transgender patients and people seeking abortion coverage lose coverage options they can use with subsidized dollars. Enrollees face new minimum premiums and administrative verification requirements.

drawbacks.text: The phasedown means the enhanced credits shrink 20% each year starting in 2028, so by 2031 enrollees would pay roughly what they did before the 2021 enhancement — the 'extension' largely schedules the premium increases it claims to prevent.

Every subsidized enrollee would pay a minimum monthly premium of $10 to $40 depending on income, and enrollment would require government-issued photo ID for each adult, adding costs and paperwork hurdles that tend to shrink enrollment.

Marketplace plans would be barred from covering gender-transition procedures, and neither marketplace plans nor the required Healthcare Affordability Accounts could use subsidized dollars for abortion or gender-transition care, removing coverage some enrollees currently hold.

Routing every premium credit through a Healthcare Affordability Account (a form of health savings account) replaces a simple monthly credit with a new account structure that enrollees must open and manage to keep their subsidy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a genuine, if shrinking, reprieve on premiums for millions of marketplace enrollees and real transparency requirements with enforceable penalties. But the design soft-pedals the phaseout rather than preventing it, adds minimum premiums and ID paperwork that push in the opposite direction, and attaches coverage restrictions that affect a narrow group of patients. The transparency title (requiring posted prices and enforcing them with daily penalties) is the most clearly consumer-protective part; the subsidy title is a negotiated drawdown rather than an extension.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced on December 9, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on December 9, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it remains.
The bill would extend enhanced ACA premium tax credits through 2031 while phasing them down 20% per year beginning in 2028 and imposing minimum monthly premiums of $10–$40 by income tier.

It would appropriate funding for cost-sharing reduction payments and $15.5 billion across fiscal years 2027–2030 for state reinsurance and high-risk-pool programs, and would toughen hospital, lab, imaging, and surgery center price transparency requirements with per-day penalties.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet — the bill has only been referred to committee, so nothing has changed for anyone. If provisions advance, insurers and states stand to gain first from the funding; enrollees gain only to the extent the subsidy provisions survive intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — it sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and it was referred to the Finance Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no votes, so no partisan pattern is visible yet.

industries.note: The bill restores and directly appropriates cost-sharing reduction payments to issuers, directs advance payments to them to lower enrollee premiums, and routes $15.5 billion in state reinsurance and market-stabilization money that flows to insurers. That locks in private insurers as the permanent channel for subsidized coverage, though parts of the money (CSR payments, reinsurance) do lower what enrollees pay, while the subsidy phasedown and minimum premiums push in the other direction.

Hospitals must post standard charges, negotiated rates, and discounted cash prices in machine-readable form, have executives attest to accuracy, and face per-day civil penalties — and must accept the discounted cash price as payment in full. Their interest in opaque pricing runs against patients comparison-shopping for care.

industries.industry: Clinical labs, imaging providers, and ambulatory surgical centers
industries.note: These providers would face new price disclosure requirements with per-day penalties starting in 2027, ending the practice of quoting unpredictable prices after the fact.

Every subsidized marketplace enrollee would be required to open and maintain a Healthcare Affordability Account, creating a large new class of health savings accounts that financial institutions administer.

Marketplace plans could not cover gender-transition procedures, subsidized dollars could not pay for abortion or gender-transition care, and federal cost-sharing money could not go to plans covering abortion except in life-saving, rape, or incest cases — narrowing the covered market for these providers and the coverage of the patients who use them.

analysis.trajectory: Introduced with one sponsor and zero cosponsors and referred to the Finance Committee, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote in that form. But enhanced ACA credits are a live political fight, and pieces of this bill — the phasedown structure, the savings-account vehicle, the reinsurance funding, the transparency title — could resurface in a larger health or appropriations package.
